llm.reply:
NCBIGene:4292 (MLH1) is linked to Muir-Torré syndrome, hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer type 2, mismatch repair cancer syndrome 1, Lynch syndrome 1, and mismatch repair cancer syndrome 2 [1][2][3][4][6][7], while NCBIGene:4436 (MSH2) appears in the graph as a gene record without a linked disease association returned here [5]. This asymmetry in the findings reflects that MLH1's role in these hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes is well documented, whereas the corresponding MSH2 disease links were not retrieved for this query.

## MLH1 function

MLH1 forms the MutL alpha complex with PMS2, which nicks DNA near mismatches to initiate repair, and this gene is described as a locus frequently mutated in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer [18: "This gene was identified as a locus frequently mutated in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC)"]. MLH1 also participates in meiotic mismatch repair and general mismatch repair processes [15][21], and is involved in the broader response to stress [26].

## Variant and functional evidence

Multiple ClinVar records catalog MLH1 sequence variants, including NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.545+1271_677+737delinsCA [10], NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.453+625_545+920delinsT [17], NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.1418A>T (p.His473Leu) [23], and NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.884+5T>A [28]. Functional assays have been used to interpret variants of uncertain significance in both MLH1 and MSH2, aiding identification of Lynch syndrome patients [22], and yeast/in vitro assays have specifically characterized MLH1 variant function [16].

## Clinical and translational context

Colorectal cancer with deficient mismatch repair has been characterized clinicopathologically and molecularly [27], and clinical trials such as MAGENTA and the IMPACT study address genetic testing and predisposition screening relevant to mismatch repair gene carriers [29][13]. A pembrolizumab trial has also targeted microsatellite-unstable tumors, a hallmark of mismatch repair deficiency [19].

MLH1 and MSH2 are both DNA mismatch repair genes whose disruption underlies hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes, linked in the graph to Muir-Torré syndrome [2], Colorectal cancer, hereditary nonpolyposis, type 2 [3], Mismatch repair cancer syndrome 1 [4], Lynch syndrome 1 [6], and Mismatch repair cancer syndrome 2 [7].

## MLH1 identity and function

MLH1 is formally named mutL homolog 1 [1], carries the gene symbol MLH1 [8], and is also referred to by the gene name MLH1 [12], with its OMIM entry titled DNA MISMATCH REPAIR PROTEIN MLH1; MLH1 [11]. Its encoded protein pairs with PMS2 to form MutL alpha, which nicks DNA near mismatches to trigger repair, and it was identified as a gene frequently mutated in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer [18: "This gene was identified as a locus frequently mutated in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC)"]. It also participates in mismatch repair [21] and meiotic mismatch repair [15] biological processes, and in response to stress [26].

## MSH2 identity

MSH2 is formally named mutS homolog 2 [5], the partner gene most often studied alongside MLH1 in Lynch syndrome variant assays [22].

## Variants and literature

ClinVar records document specific MLH1 variants, including NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.545+1271_677+737delinsCA [10], NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.453+625_545+920delinsT [17], NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.1418A>T (p.His473Leu) [23], and NM_000249.4(MLH1):c.884+5T>A [28]. Functional studies have assessed MLH1 variant effects using yeast and in vitro repair assays [16] and methylation tolerance assays covering both MLH1 and MSH2 to identify Lynch syndrome patients [22], alongside work on deficient mismatch repair colorectal cancer characterization [27] and MLH1 and longevity [9], corresponding to PubMed IDs 16474933 [14], 17510385 [20], 30998989 [25], and 36150551 [30].

## Clinical trials

Several trials address MLH1/MSH2-related cancer risk, including the IMPACT Study on genetic predisposition to prostate cancer [13], a study of MK-3475 in microsatellite unstable tumors [19], a trial on surgery to prevent ovarian cancer in patients with genetic mutations [24], and the Stand Up to Cancer MAGENTA genetic testing accessibility study [29].
